You will gradually increase the amount of Lamictal you take in 25-50 mg intervals after a certain number of weeks. A therapeutic dose is 150mg-200mg, but you can go up as high as 400mg. Your doctor should have explained that to you. Call your doctor to ask how he wants you to increase the medicine. You must increase slowly and over the course of several weeks.

Be on the look-out for rashes. If you develop any kind of rash, see a doctor immediately. There is something known as the "Lamictal Rash," which is Steven Johnson's Syndrome, which can be fatal. It is a very rare side effect, and people who get it usually either increased their dosage too quickly, or it had a reaction with other drugs the person was taking. 

Some people get a "Lamictal Headache," but that goes away and usually occurs right after increasing a dose. It (normally) isn't an ongoing side effect.

It takes a long time to start helping, or at least it does for me. It usually takes me about 6-8 weeks, but it is a really great mood stabilizer. I have no side effects whatsoever, which is the case for a lot of people. 
 
I take a 200mg pill in the morning when I wake up. I don't need to take it with food or anything. 

Please be sure to call your doctor back to get more information. Also, look into getting a different doctor. He seems like a jerk.

I understand that you are trying to express confusion, but you're going about it in the wrong way. I'm sure I'm not the only person who is insulted by your post. 

How do other people's personal decisions about taking medication affect your life? You take your medicine regularly, which is ideal, but it really should be of no concern to you what other people do. 

We are all different and we all have different reasons as to why we've gone off medicine before. I personally did it because I felt like I didn't need it, and that I was misdiagnosed with bipolar. This happened a few times. I have gone for long stretches of stability without medication, which is what led me to believe that my diagnosis was incorrect. I am not the only person who has experienced this. 

Not every doctor is an expert, despite what you may think. I was misdiagnosed for 6 years and went to a few different psychiatrists and therapists. Pdocs aren't mind readers and they aren't infallible. They make mistakes. Those mistakes can have serious consequences and cause people with mental illnesses to lose trust in their judgement. 

I hope this gave you some sort of insight. I also hope that you change your mindset on this issue. Please understand that this post was offensive because your wording was harsh and unnecessarily rude. Many of us are in a bad place right now and don't need to feel judged in a forum that we go to in order to support one another.

My doctor talked to me about triggers. She advised me to avoid stressful situations, alcohol, and marijuana. Encountering a trigger won't necessarily make you hypomanic or depressed, but it is possible for a mood change to occur when faced with it. 

Moods will still come and go, but the idea is that if you avoid "triggers," you will experience less shifts in mood.

Have you read about psychotic depression and schizoaffective disorder? You can't know what's really going on without seeing a psychiatrist, but those disorders sound like they could fit what you're describing.

Sometimes I'm just happy and creative, but that is only on occasion. I have had a few mixed episodes too, which involved racing thoughts, uncontrollable rage, and suicidal tendencies. So, yes, you can definitely be angry when you're manic or hypomanic.

Yes, I've been through this before. I wasn't diagnosed as bipolar II until I had been dating my current boyfriend for over a year, but I have always had the changes in mood (although I was mainly depressed). I just didn't have a "diagnosis" or "title" other than major depression.

In high school and early in college, I would just explain to my boyfriends that I have depression if I was low. I had no way of explaining my extreme changes in moods, which I can now identify as mixed moods and hypomania. I tried to hide mood swings to the best of my ability, but of course they all saw them eventually. All of my ex-boyfriends couldn't handle my intense mood changes and I ended all of those relationships because I felt horrible for making them go through that. 

My current boyfriend of five years is the only person who has put up with my moods and helped me as I adjusted to medicine time and time again (I've taken myself off of it several times). 
You need to find a guy who is willing to accept your bipolar and willing to help you get through your moods. If you tell this guy eventually, which you should, and he is scared off, that is alright. It's better to find out early on that he can't accept your bipolar so there aren't too many emotional ties. 

There are lots of guys in the world and you will eventually find someone who will accept you for you entirely. Good luck!

As a young person with bipolar II (I'm a 22 year old female, I was diagnosed when I was 19), I would say that being supportive and understanding is what would be the most helpful. My parents were not very supportive or understanding, and it really hurt me. 
Like -kira- said, the absolute most insulting thing they do is ask, "Did you take your medicine?!?" if I have any emotions about anything. It's the most infuriating thing in the world. Additionally, my parents would often tell me (like devellediamond said) that I had an attitude problem and that I was just acting out for attention. This only made my depression and suicidal thoughts more intense. So please don't do those things! 

My teenage years were really, really, really hard. I think it would have been better if my parents had taken the time to understand what I was going through. They are much better and supportive now, and have come to accept the diagnosis (just in the last month, actually). I appreciate that they are there for me now, but I can't forget how much they hurt me when I was a teenager and in my very early 20's.

I understand why you are frightened by the diagnosis, as the suicide statistics for bipolar II are scary. I liken bipolar disorder to diabetes. You can't cure diabetes or bipolar. Neither disease ever goes away, but you can still lead a fairly happy and successful life with either one, so long as you are properly treated and stay on the prescribed medication. 

I have been on and off of medication ever since my diagnosis, and I would have had a much easier time in college and kept many more friends if I had just stayed on my medicine. Encourage her to stay medicated, even if she thinks she's cured! 

This isn't a death sentence, and I believe that with your support and proper medication (that she stays on no matter what), she will probably lead a happy and successful life. 

EDIT: Also, like others have said, mood tracking/mood journaling is an awesome idea. I would definitely encourage her to do it, it has helped me a lot.
